nodes.body:
The clearance notice went up on the tide tower door in the first week of March. Ferry Bend was sealing the tower for repairs, and until then the warden wanted hands to help clear the old works out.

Under the words ran a column of small flag hoists inked in pairs, which was the tower's own way of numbering things. A line at the bottom gave the rule: add the moon day to the posted hour, and carry past twelve. Nobody had worked a single hoist out yet.

Bex whistled, and Jun said, "We should sign on."

"All three of us," you said. "Nobody clears a tower alone."

choices.label: Read the notice together

nodes.body:
Signing on was easy, but doing the actual work was the part that needed a plan.

You met on the towpath after school with three sets of gloves and one lamp, while across the lock the tower stood quiet with the notice still flapping on its door.

Bex had copied the hoist column into a school book. "The numbering means something," she said. "If we read it, we know what is worth saving."

Jun kept looking at the walls instead. "Or we find our own way in and get started."

You were looking at the warden's hut, where a light was burning, and asking outright was a plan too, probably the strangest of them.

choices.label: Study the hoist column first
Watch the tower for a way in
Knock at the warden's hut

nodes.body:
Bex spread the copied column across the lock beam. Every hoist gave a number and an hour, and the rule sat underneath: add the moon day, then carry past twelve.

The moon day was five, and hoist one read ten. Ten and five made fifteen, and past twelve that landed on three. Shelf three held gate pins, exactly as promised. Hoist two read nine, which made fourteen, so shelf two.

It was slow work, but honest. One entry carried two flags instead of one: Maren's tide clock, unfinished. A margin note travelled with it: winding the counterweight to its top mark lifts the loft hatch, and the crank for it hangs on shelf three.

choices.label: Look along shelf three first
Reach for the counterweight now

nodes.body:
You walked the whole outside of the tower at low water, twice.

The main door was locked and the ground floor windows were barred. Then Jun crouched down at the bank and pointed. The old sluice culvert ran under the wall, a square brick throat wide enough to walk through in a stoop, and it had been dry for years, ever since the new channel took the flow.

Nothing here was broken, and nothing here was even hidden. It had only been forgotten, and you were the first ones in a long while to look.

At the far end a grate stood ajar, and above it an iron ladder climbed to the loft window.

choices.label: Push through the culvert grate
Climb the ladder to the window

nodes.body:
The warden's hut smelled of tar and tea, and Warden Bly listened with her arms folded while you asked to join the clearance crew.

"You know it is work, not a treasure hunt," she said.

"We know that," Bex answered, steadily enough that nobody said it twice.

Bly considered the three of you for a long moment, then took her oar down off the wall. She rowed you across herself, carried the oar over her shoulder up the steps, and let you in through the winch loft.

"This tower was Maren's," she said. "She built the tide clock and never got to finish it, and there is more to that story if you want it."

choices.label: Pull your gloves on now
Listen to Bly's account first

nodes.body:
Shelf three was in the boat shed, exactly where the numbering promised it would be.

Bex went along the shelves with the lamp, past trays of gate pins sorted by size. Behind them, wrapped in oiled cloth, lay the winch crank: a bent iron handle with a square socket, the one part missing from the loft.

Nobody had hidden it. Somebody had simply put it where the index said it belonged, years ago, and there it had stayed ever since.

"The system is honest," Jun said, which felt like the important thing to learn tonight.

The crank came up cold, and heavier than it looked.

choices.label: Turn the crank until it lifts

nodes.body:
Bly set the lamp on a barrel and settled onto the step beside it.

"Maren ran this tower for thirty years," she said. "She built the tide clock so anybody could tell when the low ford was walkable. Cart drivers and old women and kids like you all looked up and knew."

Then the new channel took the flow, trade moved away, and the town stopped looking up.

"She kept working anyway," Bly said. "Numbered every part in her own code, and she was still numbering the winter she stopped."

She stood up and brushed off her knees before she added, "That clock has read wrong for eleven years, and it bothers me."

choices.label: Carry her account up the stair

nodes.body:
The ladder was iron and short, maybe two floors, with rungs as thick as your wrist. Bex went first while Jun stood underneath with his hands up, and you held the lamp steady on the rungs.

The loft window had lost its catch years ago, and it swung inward the moment Bex pushed at it.

One at a time you climbed through onto the loft floor, which was solid boards, thick dust, and the smell of old rope. Nobody hurried, and nobody let go until the next hand had hold.

You were in. Below the loft hatch, a ladder ran down into the dark working floor.

choices.label: Drop down to the working floor

nodes.body:
Inside, the tower was one tall room with its floors stacked up like shelves.

The clearance list was nailed by the stair, and it divided the whole job into four: the catwalk up top, where the hoist mast came through the roof; the warden's office, stuffed with paper; the tail-race door, where the moving works ran under the weir; and the pump cellar, down where the tide engine lived.

Four rooms, three of you, and one evening before the horns sounded.

"Split up?" Jun said.

"No," said Bex. "One at a time, all of us together."

The only question left was which one.

choices.label: Climb to the hoist catwalk
Push open the office door
Listen at the tail-race door
Feel down to the pump cellar

nodes.body:
The catwalk stair climbed in tight turns and came out into wind and river light.

Twelve hoist levers stood in a row, numbered one to twelve, and the handles were polished by years of hands, though not evenly. Lever five shone, and so did ten, and then three, and then eight. Bex traced along them with one finger. "Five each time," she said, "and when it runs past twelve it begins again at one."

On the door frame beside her, keepers had scratched their initials shoulder high, one under another, for a hundred years.

Under the last lever sat a brass pointer in oilcloth, as long as your arm.

choices.label: Carry the pointer down the stair

nodes.body:
The office was nothing but paper. Toll ledgers stood in waterproof bindings, every cargo and every flood of eighty years ruled out in red.

Through the window you could hear the weir gates working: long, long, short, then long, long, short again. Bex found the identical run in the ledger's flag column, drawn in the margin with the sum worked beside it. Hour plus moon day, carried past twelve. Some clerk had done it a thousand times.

In the desk drawer lay a toothed wheel, labelled in Maren's handwriting.

Jun stood looking at the shelves. "Somebody should catalogue these properly," he said, and he meant it.

choices.label: Take the wheel to the bench
Open the ledgers and start listing

nodes.body:
The tail-race door opened off the winch loft, and pinned by the lamp hooks was Maren's own drawing: a gate in cross section, with tide sums worked into the margin beside each hoist. Hour, moon day, carry.

Below the loft, the tunnel ran dry and black underneath the weir. Light wells dropped pale squares onto the floor every forty paces, and you counted them out loud as you went.

At the second well a stub axle sat in a wall niche, and Bex pocketed it.

At the third, the lamp reached far enough to show the drive drum lying at the tunnel's end, past a long stretch with no light in it at all.

choices.label: Feel your way to the drum
Look at the dark stretch honestly

nodes.body:
The pump cellar was cool and dim, and the whole of it was moving.

The tide engine racks rose and eased along the wall as the river breathed against the gates, and standing beside them felt like standing beside something asleep. Nobody was frightened of it. You simply wanted to watch it for a while.

Numbers were stamped up the side of every rack to mark the depth, and Jun read them off with the lamp. Three, eight, one, six. "It climbs by five," he said, "and past twelve it wraps around again."

Behind the last rack, half under a tarp, lay a brass yoke with Maren's number punched into the end.

choices.label: Haul the yoke up the stair

nodes.body:
The assembly bench stood on the working floor, under the tide clock's mount.

The mount had twelve seats around it, numbered like a dial, and Maren's fitting diagram hung above the bench. It used the tower's rule, the same rule printed everywhere in this building: take the posted hour, add the moon day, and carry past twelve. The slate by the door was chalked for today, hour ten and moon day five.

The piece sat waiting on the bench.

Jun wanted to read the diagram and place it properly. Bex thought it would go in if pushed. There was a seam in the panel behind the bench. Or you could pick a seat and try.

choices.label: Read the diagram, then seat it
Push the piece in hard
Feel along the seam behind
Pick a seat and try

nodes.body:
Jun worked the sum out loud so everybody could check it. Ten for the hour, five for the moon day, which makes fifteen, and fifteen is past twelve, so you keep counting: one, two, three.

Seat three.

You turned the piece until its lug lined up and let it down, and it went in the way a key goes into a lock that likes it. No force, no wobble, one small click.

Then the mount moved. All twelve seats turned a quarter together, took up the slack, and held. Behind the bench a latch let go with a sound like a swallowed cough, and the whole back wall swung an inch out.

choices.label: Push the bench wall open

nodes.body:
Bex leaned her weight on it, and the piece went halfway in and stopped, and the mount locked up with a dull knock.

Nobody said anything unkind about it. Everybody had wanted it to work.

The mount was not broken. It had done exactly the thing it was built to do, which was refuse. The lug sat cocked in its seat, and the slack had gone out of the whole ring.

Screwed to the bench frame was a brass plate carrying the tower's standing rule, the same rule posted down at the racks: ease back a quarter turn before asking a full one.

Which is patience, spelled out in brass.

choices.label: Ease it back a quarter turn
Set the piece down for tonight

nodes.body:
The panel behind the bench came away with two fingers and no tools at all, because Maren had meant it to.

Inside sat a slate about the size of a book, with a short column of flag hoists chalked onto it. The code was the same as everything else in the tower, only quicker: four lines instead of forty.

Bex ran it in her head. "Hour plus moon day, carry." Two of the lines pointed the same way, at the strongroom door under the stair, and the third pointed somewhere nobody had ever mentioned, a room with no number on the clearance list at all.

Jun grinned. "A catalogue inside the catalogue."

choices.label: Trace the lines to the strongroom
Follow the line nobody catalogued

nodes.body:
The strongroom was smaller than you expected, and considerably fuller.

On the table lay Maren's last workbook, open, ending in a letter. Keep the river honest, it asked, and that was the whole of the request.

Beside it sat a small tin whistle she had made herself, worn smooth at the mouth, and along the wall stood crates of town property: gauge plates, brass rule bars, the settlement's own stock, logged and dusty.

Three of you, two hands each. The first closing horn would sound in minutes, and after the horns the tower was sealed.

It was more than you could carry out, and that was the plain fact of it.

choices.label: Carry the piece out for the town
Pocket the whistle, log the rest
Load your arms with all of it

nodes.body:
You never got past the second shelf, and you did not mind in the slightest.

The ledgers went back eighty years. Bex started a proper list of year, binding, and contents, while Jun read out the flood of 1911 in a voice that made it sound like weather happening now. You did the numbering, and an hour in you finally understood something the whole crew had missed. The tower's code was never a lock. It was a catalogue, and every hoist told you where a thing lived, and the ledgers had been using it the entire time.

Then a lamp came up the stair. Warden Bly did not shout at anybody. She looked at the page you were on, slid a scrap of card in to hold the place, and closed the book gently.

"Closing," she said. "Come back Saturday. Nobody touches these shelves before then, and I will see to that."

Outside, the river lay flat and orange. You had cleared nothing and learned everything, and the ledgers would still be waiting.

You stood at the edge of the dark stretch and looked at it honestly.

No light wells for forty paces, wet brick underfoot in places, and a heavy drum that would take two of you carrying it blind under a low roof.

Bex said it first. "If somebody turns an ankle in there, the drum still stays put, and now one of us is limping home." Nobody argued with her, because it was not a brave speech and it did not need to be one.

So you called it off, marking the spot with a chalk arrow on the brick, writing the count of paces beside it, and walking back toward the light wells at an ordinary speed.

Jun stayed quiet along the towpath until he said, "We could bring proper lamps."

"And rope," said Bex.

The tide clock stayed unfinished. The tunnel was still there, and so were you, and those two facts fit together perfectly well.

You picked seat seven because seven felt right.

The piece went in and sat there doing absolutely nothing. No click, no take up. You tried nine, and then four, and the mount allowed it, which was somehow worse than being refused. A machine built for reading does not argue with a guess; it simply waits.

Outside, the first closing horn carried across the water, and the second came right behind it.

Bex checked the slate by the door. Hour ten, moon day five, sitting there in chalk the whole evening. "It was on the wall," she said. Nobody groaned, because everybody was too busy feeling silly.

You lifted the piece out, wrapped it, and left it on the bench where the crew would find it. Nothing was bent and nothing was lost. The tower simply closed with the fit still unmade, and that is what guessing costs at a bench built to be read.

The mount held the piece the way a door holds a coat: not open, not shut, and not moving.

You tried the quarter turn back and it would not come. Jun found the linkage bent a hair out of true, which is the sort of thing a flat spanner fixes in a minute and fingers never fix at all.

Then Warden Bly's lamp came up the stair, and she read the bench in a single look.

"The rule is posted," she said, and it was: no forcing after dark. "It holds for me as well. I have broken more in the last hour of a day than in all the rest of it."

So you stopped. You wrote the fault on the bench slate in plain words, so the next pair of hands would know exactly what they were meeting.

Walking home, Jun was already listing tools and Bex was already arguing about which ones. Tomorrow had a plan in it.

The line nobody catalogued led to a stair nobody had swept, and at the top of it stood a door with no lock on it at all.

Maren's workshop was not a museum. It was a room in the middle of being used, with half made parts laid along the bench in the order she had left them, and a drawing pinned to the wall with its final line unfinished.

Then Bex pushed the roof hatch open and stopped.

Reeds. A whole shallow garden of them, green as anything on the bank, growing in a tray of river mud on the flat lead roof. Above the tray a cistern pipe let one drop fall, and then another, and then another, about as slow as a resting heartbeat. Maren had built it to keep watering long after she was done watering it.

Nobody said the word out loud. It simply became true, the three of you standing up there in the wet reed smell with the town below.

Somebody had to keep this room going, and it was going to be you.

You carried the piece out in Jun's coat, and everything else stayed exactly where it was, written down in Bly's ledger in your own handwriting.

Fitting it took a fortnight and three adults who knew what they were doing. Then, on a wet Tuesday, the tide clock's hand came off eleven years of stuck and moved.

Nobody made a speech about it. The clerk entered a single line in the town register: tide clock, restored, held for the public. That was the whole of the ceremony.

By the end of the month, though, people were looking up again. Cart drivers checked the hand before they took the low ford, and old Mr. Sayer said it was the first honest thing the river had told him since the channel changed.

Maren left the clock unfinished because she ran out of years, not because she gave up, and you understood that now in a way no notice could have taught you.

The three of you never really stopped being a crew after that.

The letter asked one thing, and you read it twice to be certain. Keep the river honest. It did not say keep nothing.

So you chose small. The tin whistle went into Bex's pocket, worn smooth where Maren's mouth had been, and everything else went back the way you found it. The crates got pushed square against the wall, and the workbook went back on the table, closed, with the letter inside it. Jun wrote the whole inventory on the bench slate, every item in plain words, so Bly would find the list before she found anything moved.

The first horn sounded and you were already on the stair.

Out on the towpath, Bex blew a single note. It was thin and low and completely unremarkable, and the three of you laughed like it was the funniest thing the river had ever done.

You told nobody. Not because it was a secret worth keeping from anyone, but because it was yours.

You took the whistle, and then you took two gauge plates, a rule bar, and the workbook as well, because your arms were right there and so was everything else.

The strongroom floor was silt, fine as flour, laid down by eighty years of river. You noticed the footprints on your third trip: yours going out loaded, yours coming back light, and a wide drag mark where a crate corner had gone through, arrow straight at the door.

The floor had written down everything you did.

Warden Bly's lamp came around the stair before you got anywhere near that door. She looked at the silt, and then she looked at your arms, and she did not raise her voice once.

"Put it back," she said. "All of it, and then we log it, and then we go home."

It took twenty minutes, and at one point Bex apologised to a crate. Bly held the lamp the whole time, and at the door she said, "Saturday. Same time."
